title: Punctuation and Usage
bigQuestion: How can a mark the size of a crumb change what a whole sentence means?

story.title: The Comma That Saves Grandma
story.kicker: One family group chat, one missing comma, and a grandmother hiding behind the couch.
paragraphs: A text goes out to a family group chat: Let's eat Grandma. Grandma reads it and, being a good sport, replies with a picture of herself hiding behind the couch. Everyone laughs. But look at what happened. One missing comma turned an invitation to dinner into a threat to eat a relative. Let's eat, Grandma, is a call to the table. Let's eat Grandma is a horror movie.

The joke is old, and it works because it is true. Punctuation is not decoration on top of words. It is part of the meaning. The comma in Let's eat, Grandma does the job your voice does when you speak: the tiny pause that says I am talking to you, not about you. Writing has no voice, so it needs marks to stand in for pauses, stops, questions, and who said what.

Consider a few more. A woman without her man is nothing. A woman: without her, man is nothing. Same nine words, opposite claims. The teacher said the student is lazy. The teacher, said the student, is lazy. Two commas, and the insult changes direction. I'm sorry I love you is an apology. I'm sorry. I love you. is a declaration. In each pair, nobody changed a word.

This chapter is about those marks and the rules around them: where commas go and where they do not, what a semicolon does that a comma cannot, how an apostrophe shows ownership, how quotation marks hand a sentence to a speaker. Then the words that sound alike but mean different things, the spelling patterns that make sense once you see them, and the guides that professional writers keep on their desks.

None of it is about being fussy. Every rule here exists because a reader once got lost, or laughed at the wrong moment, or had to read a sentence three times. You will learn the rules so that your readers never have to. And you will learn that when the rules bend, they bend for a reason.
story.think: Think of a text message you once misread because of a missing mark or a strange pause. What did you think it meant, and what did it really mean?

lessons.title: Series and Introductory Commas
lessons.mainIdea: Use commas to separate items in a series and to set off an introductory word, phrase or clause from the main sentence.
reading: Read this shopping list in sentence form: We need eggs milk bread and peanut butter. Your eye stumbles. Now with commas: We need eggs, milk, bread, and peanut butter. Each item stands apart. A list of three or more items inside a sentence is a *series*, and commas are the walls between the items.

The comma before the and in a series has a name, the *serial comma*, and it is a real argument among editors. Newspapers usually skip it. Books usually keep it. Both are accepted styles, but the safe rule for school is to use it, because it prevents misreadings. Compare: I thanked my parents, Ms. Ruiz and Mr. Bell. Without the last comma, a reader might think Ms. Ruiz and Mr. Bell are your parents.

The second job of the comma is to mark the end of an *introductory element*, whatever comes before the main clause. A single word: However, the bus was late. A phrase: After the last bell, the halls emptied. A dependent clause: When the storm hit, the lights went out. The comma tells the reader: the setup is over, here comes the main idea.

For very short introductory phrases, the comma is optional: At noon we ate. Many writers still include it, and no one will mark it wrong. When in doubt, read the sentence aloud. If you hear a pause after the opener, put the comma there. If a missing comma could cause a stumble, as in After eating the dog fell asleep, the comma is not optional at all.

words.d: a list of three or more items inside one sentence
the comma before and or or in a series; also called the Oxford comma
a word, phrase or dependent clause that comes before the main clause of a sentence

look.title: The Comma That Splits a Family
look.text: A student wrote in a thank-you note: This trip was made possible by my grandparents, Coach Diaz and the school nurse. Coach Diaz read it and asked, with a grin, when he had become a grandparent.
look.prompt: Explain the misreading. Where does one comma need to go, and does it change the number of people the student is thanking?

check.q: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a series?
choices: We packed tents, sleeping bags, and a lantern.
We packed, tents, sleeping bags, and a lantern.
We packed tents sleeping bags and a lantern.
We packed tents, and sleeping bags, and, a lantern.
check.why: Commas go between the items, with the serial comma before and. No comma belongs after packed.

check.q: Where does the comma go in After the game ended the parking lot emptied?
check.why: After the game ended is the introductory clause. The comma marks its end, before the main clause begins.

check.q: What does the comma after an introductory clause tell the reader?
choices: That the sentence is a question
That the setup is over and the main idea is coming
check.why: The comma separates the opener from the main clause so the reader knows where the main idea begins.

lessons.title: Extra Information Commas
lessons.mainIdea: Set off with commas any clause or phrase that only adds information; leave out the commas when the words are needed to tell which one.
reading: Two sentences, one comma apart. My brother who lives in Peoria is a nurse. My brother, who lives in Peoria, is a nurse. In the first, you have more than one brother, and the clause tells the reader which one: the Peoria brother. In the second, you have one brother, and the clause simply adds a fact about him. The commas change how many brothers you have.

A clause that is needed to identify the noun is *restrictive*. It restricts, or narrows, which one you mean. No commas. A clause that only adds information is *nonrestrictive*. You could lift it out and the sentence would still point at the same person or thing. Commas on both sides, like handles on a basket.

A quick test: cross out the clause and ask if the sentence still means what you meant. Students who cheat will fail. Cross out who cheat and you get Students will fail, which is not the claim. Restrictive, no commas. The gym, which was built in 1962, needs a new roof. Cross out the middle and you still know which gym. Nonrestrictive, commas.

Many careful writers use that for restrictive clauses and which, with commas, for nonrestrictive ones: the book that I lost; the book, which I lost. This is a common style rule, not an iron law, but following it makes your meaning clearer. The same comma logic applies to an *appositive*, a noun that renames another noun: My friend Sam is here (which friend: Sam) versus Sam, my oldest friend, is here (extra information).

words.d: describes a clause or phrase that is needed to tell which one; it takes no commas
describes a clause or phrase that only adds information; it is set off with commas
a noun or noun phrase placed next to another noun to rename or explain it

look.title: Two Dogs, Two Rules
look.text: The dog that bit the mail carrier lives on Elm Street. Our dog, who has never bitten anyone, sleeps under the porch all day.
look.prompt: Why does the first sentence have no commas while the second has two? What would change if you added commas to the first?

check.q: Drivers who text are dangerous. Why are there no commas?
choices: Because who is never set off with commas
Because the clause tells which drivers, so it is restrictive
Because the sentence is too short
check.why: Not all drivers are dangerous; the clause narrows it to the ones who text. A restrictive clause takes no commas.

check.q: Which sentence means you have only one sister?
choices: My sister who plays soccer is tall.
My sister that plays soccer is tall.
My sister, who plays soccer, is tall.
My sisters who play soccer are tall.
check.why: The commas make the clause extra information. Without them, the clause would be picking one sister out of several.

check.q: What is an appositive?
choices: A verb that shows a wish
A clause that begins with because
A noun that renames another noun beside it
check.why: In Sam, my oldest friend, is here, the phrase my oldest friend renames Sam. That is an appositive.

lessons.title: Commas Between Adjectives
lessons.mainIdea: Put a comma between two adjectives when each describes the noun equally and could be joined by and; do not use one when the first adjective describes the second plus the noun.
reading: A cold, gray morning. A big red truck. Why does one pair get a comma and the other not? Say and between them. A cold and gray morning sounds fine. A big and red truck sounds odd. Now swap them. A gray, cold morning works. A red big truck does not. When both tests pass, the adjectives are *coordinate adjectives*, equal partners, and they take a comma.

When the tests fail, the adjectives are *cumulative adjectives*: they stack. Big describes red truck as one unit. The first adjective is really describing the second plus the noun. Cumulative adjectives usually follow an order that English speakers feel without thinking: opinion, size, age, shape, color, origin, material. A lovely little old round blue Italian wooden box. No commas anywhere.

Two more comma rules follow the same logic of equal partners. Do not put a comma between the last adjective and the noun: a cold, gray, morning is wrong. And do not put a comma between a subject and its verb, no matter how long the subject is: The long, tired line of students outside the cafeteria, finally moved is wrong. Subject and verb are a team, not a list.

Why does it matter? Comma-heavy writing feels choppy, and a comma in the wrong spot makes readers hunt for a list that is not there. Comma-light writing lets adjectives blur together. The and test takes two seconds and works almost every time. Use it whenever you have stacked two describing words.

words.d: two adjectives that describe a noun equally; they can be joined by and or swapped, and take a comma
adjectives that stack, the first describing the second plus the noun; they take no comma

look.title: And or Not
look.text: Six noun phrases from a story: a dark, empty hallway; a small plastic cup; three loud kids; a sweet, sharp smell; an old brick school; a soft, warm blanket.
look.prompt: Apply the and test and the swap test to each one. Which ones need their comma, and would any of them be wrong with a comma?

check.q: Which is punctuated correctly?
check.why: A tall and wooden fence sounds odd, and a wooden tall fence sounds wrong. The adjectives stack, so no comma.

check.q: Which test tells you two adjectives are coordinate?
choices: They both start with the same letter
They come before a plural noun
You can put and between them and swap their order
check.why: Coordinate adjectives are equal partners, so and fits between them and the order does not matter.

check.q: Which sentence has a comma error?
choices: The old, rusty bike, sat in the yard.
The old, rusty bike sat in the yard.
The bike, which was old and rusty, sat in the yard.
The bike sat in the old, rusty yard.
check.why: The comma after bike splits the subject from its verb. Subject and verb are a team, never separated by a lone comma.

lessons.title: Semicolons and Colons
lessons.mainIdea: A semicolon joins two closely related independent clauses; a colon follows a complete sentence to introduce a list, an explanation or a quotation.
reading: The power went out; the whole block went quiet. A period would work here, but it would separate two moments that belong together. A comma alone would be a splice. The *semicolon* sits between: a stop, but a soft one, used between two independent clauses. Test it by covering the semicolon. If both sides could be sentences, the semicolon is legal.

Semicolons have a second job: sorting a list whose items already contain commas. We visited Springfield, Illinois; Madison, Wisconsin; and Des Moines, Iowa. With commas alone, a reader might count six places instead of three. The semicolons act as bigger walls between the bigger pieces.

The *colon* points forward. It says: here comes what I promised. Before it, a complete sentence. After it, a list, an explanation or a quotation. She packed three things: a flashlight, a map and her father's compass. He had one rule: never lie to the crew. The colon says pay attention, what follows is the payoff.

The most common colon error is putting it after a verb or a preposition, where nothing is complete yet: She packed: a flashlight, a map and a compass. The words before the colon are not a sentence, so the colon has nothing to stand on. Take it out, or rewrite the opener as a full sentence. And do not use a semicolon where a colon belongs; a semicolon never introduces a list.

words.d: the mark ; that joins two related independent clauses or separates list items that contain commas
the mark : that follows a complete sentence and introduces a list, an explanation or a quotation

look.title: Counting the Places
rows: Commas if only commas are used
Names a reader might count with commas only
look.cite: counted for this lesson, from the Springfield, Madison and Des Moines sentence
look.prompt: With commas only, the list has five commas and looks like six names. How do two semicolons bring the count back to three?

check.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
choices: We need; eggs, milk and bread.
After the show ended; we walked home.
We need three things; eggs, milk and bread.
The show ended; we walked home.
check.why: Both sides of the semicolon are independent clauses. The others put it after a fragment or use it to introduce a list.

check.q: Which colon is correct?
choices: Bring these: a pencil, a ruler and a calculator.
Bring: a pencil, a ruler and a calculator.
You should bring a pencil, a ruler: and a calculator.
Bring a: pencil, ruler and calculator.
check.why: Bring these is a complete sentence, so the colon can introduce the list that follows.

check.q: Why use semicolons in We stopped in Joliet, Illinois; Gary, Indiana; and Toledo, Ohio?
choices: Because semicolons are fancier than commas
Because the items already contain commas
Because place names always take semicolons
check.why: Each item has its own comma between city and state. Semicolons keep the three places from blurring into six names.

lessons.title: Dashes and Parentheses
lessons.mainIdea: Dashes and parentheses both set off an interruption; a dash makes it loud and sudden, while parentheses make it quiet and aside.
reading: Three ways to drop the same fact into a sentence. My uncle, who never cooks, made dinner. My uncle (who never cooks) made dinner. My uncle—who never cooks—made dinner. The commas are neutral. The *parentheses* whisper the fact, as if the writer leaned over to mutter it. The *dash* pair shouts it. The words are the same; the marks set the volume.

A dash is typed as two hyphens with no spaces, or as the long line called an *em dash*. Use a pair to set off an interruption in the middle of a sentence. Use a single dash to add a sharp turn at the end: The test had twenty questions—all essay. A dash breaks the flow on purpose. Use it when you want the reader to feel the break.

Parentheses hold information the sentence could live without: a date, a definition, a quick example, a side comment. The museum opened in 1893 (the year of the World's Fair) on the lakefront. If the words inside form a whole sentence on their own, put the period inside. If not, the period goes after the closing mark. Nothing inside parentheses should change the grammar of the sentence around it.

Both marks lose their power when overused. A page full of dashes reads like someone who cannot finish a thought. A page full of parentheses reads like someone who keeps whispering. Try this: use no more than one dash pair per paragraph, and ask of every parenthesis whether the fact belongs in the sentence, in a footnote, or nowhere.

words.d: the curved marks ( ) that set off a quiet aside or extra detail
a long horizontal mark that sets off a sudden interruption or a sharp turn at the end of a sentence
the full-length dash, about as wide as the letter M, typed as two hyphens on many keyboards

look.title: A Poet Who Chose Dashes
look.text:
Because I could not stop for Death—
He kindly stopped for me—
The Carriage held but just Ourselves—
And Immortality.
look.cite: Emily Dickinson, opening stanza of Because I could not stop for Death, written about 1863, published 1890
look.prompt: Dickinson ends nearly every line with a dash instead of a comma or period. Read it aloud, pausing at each dash. What does the dash do to the pace that a period would not?

check.q: What is the main difference between dashes and parentheses?
choices: Dashes make the interruption loud; parentheses make it quiet
Dashes are for lists; parentheses are for dates
Parentheses are never used in essays
check.why: Both set off an interruption. The dash draws attention to it; the parentheses tuck it away.

check.q: Which sentence uses a dash well?
choices: There was only one thing left to do—run.
check.why: A single dash near the end sets up a sharp turn: the payoff word run. The others break the sentence for no reason.

check.q: Where does the period go in a sentence that ends with a short parenthetical phrase like (see page 4)?
check.why: The phrase is not a whole sentence, so the main sentence's period comes after the closing mark.

lessons.title: Apostrophes
lessons.mainIdea: An apostrophe shows ownership or a missing letter; it never makes a word plural.
reading: The dogs bowl. The dog's bowl. The dogs' bowl. Three versions, three meanings. The first is a mistake: it says the dogs bowl, as in a bowling alley. The second is one dog and its bowl. The third is a bowl shared by several dogs. The little mark moves, and the number of dogs changes. That mark is the *apostrophe*, and it has exactly two jobs.

Job one is *possession*, showing that something belongs to someone. Add an apostrophe and s to a singular noun: the girl's coat, Chris's locker. For a plural noun that already ends in s, add only the apostrophe: the girls' coats, the players' bench. For a plural that does not end in s, add apostrophe and s: the children's room, the men's team.

Job two is the *contraction*: the apostrophe stands where letters were removed. Do not becomes don't. It is becomes it's. They are becomes they're. This is where the most common error in English lives. It's always means it is or it has. Its, with no apostrophe, is the possessive, like his and her: The dog wagged its tail. If you can swap in it is, use the apostrophe. If not, do not.

The one thing an apostrophe never does is make a plural. Signs everywhere get this wrong: Banana's 99 cents. Two DVD's. The bananas do not own anything. Plain s makes plurals: bananas, DVDs, the 1990s. When you see an apostrophe, ask which of the two jobs it is doing. If it is doing neither, delete it.

words.d: the mark ' that shows possession or stands in for missing letters
ownership or belonging: the girl's coat means the coat belongs to the girl
a shortened form of two words, such as don't or it's, with an apostrophe for the missing letters

look.title: Fix the Store Signs
look.text: A pet store sign reads: Dog's toys 50% off. Cat's and bird's too! Inside, another sign says: Its a great day to adopt. The manager wants to sell toys for many dogs, cats and birds.
look.prompt: Fix each sign. For each apostrophe you add or remove, name the job it is doing, or say why it was wrong.

check.q: Which is correct?
check.why: Its shows possession with no apostrophe. It's would mean it is, which makes no sense here.

check.q: How do you show that a bench belongs to several players?
check.why: Players is a plural ending in s, so only an apostrophe is added after it.

check.q: What is wrong with Apple's for sale?
choices: The apostrophe wrongly makes a plural; it should be Apples
check.why: The apples do not own anything and nothing is missing. A plain s makes the plural.

lessons.title: Quotation Marks
lessons.mainIdea: Quotation marks wrap a speaker's exact words and the titles of short works; commas and periods go inside the closing mark, and a new speaker starts a new paragraph.
reading: Look at a line of dialogue: "We're going to be late," Maya said, grabbing her keys. The *quotation marks* wrap only the words Maya actually spoke. The comma after late sits inside the closing mark, which is the American rule for commas and periods. The *dialogue tag*, Maya said, tells who spoke and stays outside the marks. This is *direct quotation*: her exact words.

Now the same idea reported instead of quoted: Maya said that they were going to be late. No quotation marks, because these are not her exact words; the pronoun changed from we to they. This is *indirect quotation*. Students often put marks around indirect speech. The test is simple: could a recorder have picked up these exact words? If not, no marks.

When the tag comes first, a comma introduces the quote: Maya said, "We're going to be late." When a quoted question ends the sentence, the question mark goes inside: Maya asked, "Are we late?" If the whole sentence is a question but the quote is not, the mark goes outside: Did Maya really say "we have time"? Each time a new person speaks, start a new paragraph, even if the line is one word.

Quotation marks also mark the titles of short works: a poem, a song, a short story, an article, an episode. Longer works that stand alone, such as a book, a movie, an album or a newspaper, are set in italics in print, or underlined by hand. So the poem "The Road Not Taken" appears in a book of Frost's poems. The marks say: this is a small piece that lives inside something bigger.

words.d: the marks " " that wrap a speaker's exact words or the title of a short work
the words such as Maya said that tell who is speaking
a speaker's exact words, set in quotation marks
a report of what someone said, not the exact words; it takes no quotation marks

look.title: Three Lines of Dialogue
look.text:
"You said you would be here at six," Dad said.
"I said around six," Ana answered. "It's six-fifteen."
Dad looked at the clock. "So it is."
look.prompt: Find every place a comma or period sits inside a closing mark. Then explain why the last line has no comma before the quotation.

check.q: Which is punctuated correctly?
check.why: A comma separates the quote from the tag, and in American style it goes inside the closing mark.

check.q: Which sentence needs no quotation marks?
choices: Ms. Lee asked, Where is your homework?
The sign in the hallway said Keep Out, in those exact words.
The coach said that practice was canceled.
check.why: That practice was canceled is a report, not the coach's exact words. Indirect quotation takes no marks.

check.q: Which title should go in quotation marks?
check.why: A song is a short work that lives inside an album. Novels, movies and newspapers stand alone and take italics.

lessons.title: Capital Letters
lessons.mainIdea: Capitalize the first word of a sentence, the pronoun I, and proper nouns, the names of specific people, places and things; leave common nouns lowercase.
reading: My aunt is a doctor at a hospital on the west side. My aunt, Dr. Amara Bell, works at Rush University Medical Center on the West Side of Chicago. In the first sentence every noun is general: an aunt, a doctor, a hospital, a side of town. In the second, each has become a specific name. A general noun is a *common noun* and stays lowercase. A specific name is a *proper noun* and gets a capital.

Proper nouns include people, cities, states, countries, streets, buildings, days, months, holidays, languages, nationalities, brand names and organizations. Tuesday, October, Halloween, Spanish, the Chicago Bears, Lake Michigan. Seasons stay lowercase: fall, winter. Directions stay lowercase when they mean a direction, drive west, but take a capital when they name a region: the West Side, the Midwest.

Titles before a name are capitalized: President Lincoln, Coach Diaz, Aunt Rosa. The same word after the name or on its own is not: the president spoke, my coach, my aunt. Family words follow the same rule. Mom is a name when you use it as one: I asked Mom. It is a common noun when a word like my sits in front of it: I asked my mom.

For titles of works, capitalize the first word, the last word, and every important word in between. Short words such as a, an, the, of, and, to and in stay lowercase unless they come first: The Call of the Wild; A Tale of Two Cities. Finally, the pronoun I is always capitalized, and so is the first word of a quoted sentence: She said, "Wait for me."

words.d: a general name for a person, place or thing, such as city or teacher; not capitalized
the specific name of a person, place or thing, such as Chicago or Ms. Lee; always capitalized

look.title: Fix the Postcard
look.text: A postcard written in a hurry: dear aunt rosa, we drove East to lake michigan on saturday. mom bought me a book called the call of the wild. next Summer i want to see the museum of science and industry. love, tomas
look.prompt: Rewrite the postcard with correct capitals. For each change, say which rule applies: sentence start, proper noun, title, or the pronoun I.

check.q: Which is capitalized correctly?
choices: We visited lake Michigan in july.
We visited Lake Michigan in July with aunt Rosa.
we visited Lake Michigan in July.
We visited Lake Michigan in July with Aunt Rosa.
check.why: Lake Michigan and July are proper nouns, and Aunt is capitalized when it is part of a name.

check.q: Which should be lowercase?
check.why: Seasons are common nouns. Days, months and holidays are proper nouns.

check.q: Which is the correct form of a book title?
check.why: First word, last word and important words are capitalized. The short word of stays lowercase.

lessons.title: Words That Sound Alike
lessons.mainIdea: Words that sound alike, such as affect and effect or than and then, are chosen by meaning and job, not by sound; a short test settles each one.
reading: The weather affected the game. The weather had an effect on the game. Both are correct, and they mean about the same thing. But swap them and both become wrong. *Affect* is almost always a verb, an action: to change something. *Effect* is almost always a noun, a thing: the result of a change. If you can put the in front of it, it is effect. If you can put will in front of it, it is affect.

Than and then get mixed up because in fast speech they sound the same. Than compares: taller than, more than, rather than. Then tells time or order: first this, then that. If the sentence is comparing two things, than. If it is telling what happened next, then. A pattern to remember: than has an a like compare; then has an e like next.

Each *homophone* family causes trouble because the ear cannot help. Their, there, they're: their shows ownership, their bikes; there points to a place or starts a sentence, over there, there is; they're is they are. To, too, two: to points toward, too means also or more than enough, two is the number. Your and you're: your shows ownership, you're is you are. For every one with an apostrophe, expand it. If you're does not become you are in the sentence, it is wrong.

A few more that trip up good writers. Accept means to receive; except means leaving out. Lose has one o and means to misplace or be beaten; loose has two and means not tight. Who's is who is; whose shows ownership. None of these can be settled by ear. Each needs the test, and the test takes a second. Keep a list of the ones you personally mix up and check for them last, after everything else in a draft is done.

words.d: a verb meaning to change or influence something
a noun meaning the result of a change
a word that sounds like another word but is spelled differently and means something different

look.title: Test Every Pair
look.text: A note passed in class: Your going to loose if you think there better then us. Its not even close, so except it. Six words in that note are the wrong twin.
look.prompt: Fix each one and name the test you used: expand the contraction, put the in front, or check whether the sentence compares or tells order.

check.q: Which is correct?
choices: The rain did not affect the game.
The rain did not effect the game.
The rain had no affect on the game.
The rain affected an effect on the game.
check.why: Affect is the verb: the rain did not change the game. Effect would be the noun, as in had no effect.

check.q: Which is correct?
choices: I would rather walk then ride.
First we ate, then we walked.
check.why: Then tells order: first eating, next walking. The others compare and need than.

check.q: What is the test for they're?
choices: Put the in front of it
Check if it points to a place
Expand it to they are and see if the sentence still works
Check if it comes before a noun
check.why: They're is a contraction of they are. If they are does not fit, you need their or there.

lessons.title: Spelling Patterns
lessons.mainIdea: Most English spelling follows patterns, such as dropping a silent e or doubling a final consonant before -ing; learn the pattern, then memorize the few words that break it.
reading: Hope, hoping. Hop, hopping. Why does one word drop a letter and the other add one? Because each is obeying a rule that keeps the vowel sound steady. The *silent e* in hope makes the o say its name. Drop the e before adding -ing and the o still sounds long, because the i takes over the job. Hop has a short o. Doubling the p walls off the vowel so it stays short. Without the doubling, hoping and hopping would look identical.

So the two rules: drop a final silent e before an ending that starts with a vowel (make, making; but hope, hopeful keeps the e because -ful starts with a consonant). Double the final consonant of a short one-syllable word with one vowel before adding -ing or -ed (run, running; stop, stopped). For longer words, double only if the last syllable is the *stressed syllable*: begin, beginning; but open, opening.

Two more patterns handle most of the rest. Change y to i when adding an ending, unless the ending is -ing: cry, cried, crying; happy, happier. And the old rhyme, i before e except after c, works for most words with the ee sound: believe, receive, ceiling. It fails for weird, seize and a few others. Rhymes like this are tools, not laws. Learn the tool, then learn each *exception* by name.

Spelling in English is messy because the language borrowed from French, Latin, Greek and German, and each brought its own habits. That is why a good speller does two things. First, knows the patterns, which cover most words. Second, keeps a personal list of the words that break them, because those are the ones spell-check will not always catch. Their and there are both spelled correctly. Only you know which one you meant.

words.d: an e at the end of a word that is not pronounced but makes the vowel before it say its name, as in hope
the part of a word you say with more force: be-GIN, O-pen
a word that does not follow the usual pattern and must be memorized

look.title: Letters Gained and Lost
look.prompt: Hope is longer than hop, but hoping is shorter than hopping. Explain what each word gained or lost, and why.

check.q: How do you spell run with -ing?
check.why: Run is a short word with one vowel, so the final n doubles to keep the u short.

check.q: Why is the e dropped in making?
choices: Because make is a short word
Because -ing starts with a vowel, and the i keeps the a long
Because all words drop e before endings
check.why: The silent e is dropped before a vowel ending. Before -ful, as in hopeful, the e stays.

check.q: Which word breaks the i before e rule?
check.why: Seize has e before i with no c. It is one of the exceptions to memorize.

lessons.title: Style Guides and Meaning
lessons.mainIdea: When rules are contested, a style guide settles them for a publication; whatever guide you follow, every mark you place changes what a reader takes from the sentence.
reading: Two teachers, two answers. One says always use the serial comma. One says never. Who is right? Both, in a sense. Where usage is genuinely divided, publications settle the question with a *style guide*: a rulebook that picks one option and asks every writer to follow it, so the whole newspaper or book or website reads as one voice. Most American newspapers follow the Associated Press guide, which skips the serial comma. Most book publishers follow the Chicago Manual of Style, which keeps it.

A style guide also decides things grammar does not: whether to write 9 or nine, e-mail or email, whether to capitalize internet. Your school may have one for essays. If it does, follow it. If it does not, choose a rule for yourself and keep it through the whole piece. *Consistency* is what readers notice. Switching styles mid-page looks like carelessness even when each choice is defensible.

Underneath all the rules is one idea: punctuation is meaning. The teacher said the student is lazy. The teacher, said the student, is lazy. Same six words, opposite insult; the commas changed who is talking. A woman without her man is nothing. A woman: without her, man is nothing. Each mark tells the reader how to group the words, and grouping is meaning.

So when you edit, do not ask only whether this comma is legal. Ask what this comma makes the reader think. Try the sentence with the mark and without it. Read both aloud. If the meaning shifts, choose the version that says what you meant. If a rule seems to forbid it, rewrite the sentence rather than let the wrong meaning stand. That is the whole art: rules in service of the reader, never the other way around.

words.d: a rulebook a publication follows so that every writer makes the same choices on contested points
making the same choice the same way every time through a piece of writing

look.title: One Sentence, Two Readings
look.text: A referee's note after a game: The player said the coach was out of line. Now move two commas in: The player, said the coach, was out of line.
look.prompt: Who is accusing whom in each version? Then find one sentence in your own writing where moving a comma would change the meaning.

check.q: What does a style guide do?
choices: Replaces grammar rules with new ones
Lists every word in the language
Settles contested choices so a publication reads as one voice
check.why: Where usage is divided, the guide picks one option and every writer for that publication follows it.

check.q: Why should a writer be consistent about the serial comma?
choices: Because only one choice is legal
Because switching mid-page looks careless to readers
check.why: Both styles are accepted, but mixing them in one piece looks like the writer was not paying attention.

check.q: The teacher, said the student, is lazy. Who is speaking?
check.why: The commas set off said the student as the tag. The student is calling the teacher lazy.

review.q: Which sentence has a correct introductory comma?
review.why: The comma marks the end of the introductory phrase, before the main clause.

review.q: Which sentence means the speaker has only one brother?
choices: My brother, who lives in Aurora, called.
My brother who lives in Aurora called.
My brother that lives in Aurora called.
The brother who lives in Aurora called.
review.why: The commas make the clause extra information, so it is not picking one brother out of several.

choices: The sky went dark; the wind picked up.
She bought; apples, pears and plums.
review.why: Both sides are independent clauses. A semicolon never introduces a list or follows a dependent clause.

choices: The team lost it's first game.
The teams' lost its first game.
The team lost its first game.
The team lost its' first game.
review.why: Its is the possessive. It's means it is, and its' is never a word.
A comma links the quote to its tag and sits inside the closing quotation mark.

choices: a direction such as north in drive north
a common noun such as city
review.why: Months are proper nouns. Seasons, plain directions and common nouns stay lowercase.

choices: The news had a big affect on her.
The news was effecting to her.
review.why: Affect is the verb. The noun would be effect, as in had a big effect.

review.q: What does a style guide settle?
choices: Contested choices such as the serial comma
Whether a fragment is a sentence
review.why: Grammar settles the first, second and fourth. A style guide picks one option where usage is divided.
